summary: The decided design is feasible, but five points need care. (1) rpi-image-gen can build it: image layouts are genimage templates inside image layers, so a third /data partition is a small custom image layer (copy of the built-in MBR 'image-rpios' layout plus one partition). Its own CI builds on GitHub's ubuntu-24.04-arm runners and on ubuntu-24.04 under QEMU. (2) Its built-in support is arm64 only. The Pi 3 device layer uses the 64-bit v8 kernel, and Pi 5 uses a different device layer with the 2712 kernel. armhf base and kernel layers exist, but there is no 32-bit device layer, so 32-bit would be a custom, unsupported path. Plan on arm64 for Pi 3/4/5. (3) With the default overlayroot=tmpfs that raspi-config sets, overlayroot rewrites /etc/fstab so every non-vfat filesystem, /data included, also gets a tmpfs overlay (recurse=1): /data writes would be lost. Use overlayroot=tmpfs:recurse=0 on the kernel command line, or mount /data with a native systemd .mount unit. (4) Every first-boot mechanism writes to the root and boot partitions: Raspberry Pi Imager customisation (firstrun.sh, cloud-init), ConditionFirstBoot units, resize and disk-ID randomisation. So ship the image with the overlay OFF, and seal it (overlay on, boot read-only, reboot) at the end of the first boot instead of pre-enabling it. (5) Imager 2.x applies OS customisation to a custom image only when it is opened through a manifest (.rpi-imager-manifest / os_list JSON) that sets init_format. For a 'Use custom' .img file it assumes 'none'. Raspberry Pi OS Trixie's auto-expand is triggered by the 'resize' token in cmdline.txt (an initramfs script grows partition 2 only, plus rpi-resize.service/systemd-growfs-root). Drop 'resize' and grow p3 yourself on first boot.

claims.claim: rpi-image-gen supports custom partition layouts. A layout is an 'image' layer containing a genimage template (genimage.cfg.in.*), a setup.sh that writes /etc/fstab, and image.yaml variables. The built-in MBR layout 'image-rpios' (image/mbr/simple_dual) defines boot (vfat, 0xC) and root (ext4, 0x83) with boot_part_size/root_part_size variables. The built-in GPT 'image-rota' layout already has six partitions, including a 'persistent' ext4 data partition. A BrewberryPi layout is a copy of simple_dual in the project's -S source directory with a third 'data' partition (ext4, label DATA, mountpoint /data) and extra fstab lines. On Pi 3, use MBR (msdos) because the Pi 3 trait does not set boot:gpt.
claims.evidence: Source of https://github.com/raspberrypi/rpi-image-gen (master, fetched 2026-10-09). image/mbr/simple_dual/image.yaml: 'X-Env-Layer-Name: image-rpios ... Raspberry Pi OS style image layout with MBR, vfat boot partition, and a root partition that can be ext4 or btrfs', vars boot_part_size/root_part_size. genimage.cfg.in.ext4: 'partition boot {... partition-type = 0xC ...} partition root {... 0x83 ... image = root.ext4}', 'image boot.vfat {... mountpoint = "/boot/firmware"}'. image/gpt/ab_userdata/genimage.cfg.in.ext4: partitions bootconfig, boot_a, boot_b, system_a, system_b, persistent ('mountpoint = "/persistent"'). getting_started.adoc: 'rpi-image-gen build -S myproject/ -c myproject/myimage.yaml'. trait/hw/device/rpi/sbc/pi4.deb822 and pi5.deb822 set '(boot:gpt)=y'; pi3.deb822 does not.

claims.claim: rpi-image-gen's ready-made device support is 64-bit only. Device layers exist for pi3, pi4, pi5, zero2w, cm4 and cm5. pi3 and pi4 require 'rpi-generic64' (v8 arm64 kernel). pi5 requires 'rpi-linux-2712'. The repository has armhf building blocks (layer 'raspbian-trixie-armhf', kernel layers linux-image-rpi-v7/v7l) but no 32-bit device family or config, and CI builds only arm64. A 32-bit Pi 3 image would need a hand-written device layer and is outside what the project tests. Also, Pi 5 uses a different kernel layer from Pi 3/4, so one config does not cover all three boards.
claims.evidence: rpi-image-gen master: device/pi3/device.yaml 'X-Env-Layer-Requires: rpi-generic64'; device/pi4/device.yaml 'Requires: rpi-generic64'; device/pi5/device.yaml 'Requires: rpi-device-base,rpi-linux-2712'; layer/rpi/device/family-generic64.yaml 'Generic Raspberry Pi device common with v8 kernel, boot firmware supporting all devices'; layer/raspbian/trixie/base-apt.yaml 'X-Env-Layer-Name: raspbian-trixie-armhf ... architectures: - armhf'; layer/rpi/device/armhf/linux-image-v7.yaml 'packages: - linux-image-rpi-v7'. A grep for armhf finds no device or config that uses these layers. README: 'runs best on a Raspberry Pi Host running up-to-date 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS'.

claims.claim: rpi-image-gen runs in GitHub Actions. Its own workflow builds trixie images natively on the hosted 'ubuntu-24.04-arm' runner and on 'ubuntu-24.04' x86 with qemu-user-static/binfmt. Officially only native Debian Bookworm/Trixie arm64 is supported; containers and QEMU work but are 'not formally supported'. The build runs as a regular user (podman unshare) and needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN-equivalent privileges for mmdebstrap's mount namespace.
claims.evidence: https://github.com/raspberrypi/rpi-image-gen/blob/master/.github/workflows/build.yml: 'build-arm64: ... runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm ... sudo ./install_deps.sh ... ./rpi-image-gen build -c ./config/trixie-minbase.yaml' and 'build-arm64-qemu: ... runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 ... sudo apt-get install -y qemu-user-static binfmt-support; sudo update-binfmts --enable qemu-aarch64'. README.adoc: 'Debian Bookworm and Trixie arm64 as the supported native hosts ... can run in containers or on non-arm64 hosts via QEMU, but those environments are not formally supported ... requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN'; 'The tool runs as a regular user and does not require root privileges.'

claims.claim: Packages, files and systemd units can be preinstalled. Use a 'packages:' list in the config, custom layers (mmdebstrap packages plus setup/customize hooks that receive the rootfs as $1), and executable hooks/customize90-* in the -S source directory. rpi-image-gen has no Podman layer; the only container-engine layer is Docker (layer/app-container/docker). A container image therefore has to be preloaded by our own hook, for example by shipping an OCI archive and running 'podman load' in a first-boot oneshot before the Quadlet unit starts, or by filling the /data partition subtree. That part is our own work, not a supported feature.
claims.evidence: getting_started.adoc: config 'packages: - wpasupplicant'; 'customize90-myscript will be automatically included based on its name, executability and location in relation to the -S source directory'. examples/custom_layers/README.md (custom layers with dependencies and variables). layer/app-container contains only docker/engine-trixie.yaml and engine-bookworm.yaml. A grep for 'podman' in layer/config yaml finds no Podman install layer. The examples oci_create/container_chroot only produce tarballs to 'podman load'/'podman import' on a host.

claims.claim: Raspberry Pi Imager 2.x can apply its OS customisation to a custom image only when the image is listed in a manifest (os_list JSON / .rpi-imager-manifest) that sets init_format. For a local 'Use custom' .img it assumes 'none' and offers no customisation. The manifest is opened by double-click, through App Options > Content Repository, or with 'rpi-imager --repo <file|URL>'. The formats need different packages in the image. 'systemd': Imager writes firstrun.sh and adds systemd.run= to cmdline.txt; the image needs /usr/lib/raspberrypi-sys-mods/imager_custom and /usr/lib/userconf-pi/userconf. 'cloudinit' / 'cloudinit-rpi': Imager writes user-data, meta-data and network-config to the boot partition and adds ds=nocloud to cmdline.txt; the image needs cloud-init and, for -rpi, rpi-cloud-init-mods. Current Raspberry Pi OS Trixie uses cloudinit-rpi. 'rpi-preseed' is a prototype and is not in the Raspberry Pi trixie arm64 archive. Every format writes to the FAT boot partition and changes the root filesystem on first boot.
claims.evidence: https://github.com/raspberrypi/rpi-imager/blob/main/doc/os_customisation_formats.md: '"init_format": "systemd" - ... (using firstrun.sh)', '"cloudinit-rpi" - ... enhanced', 'When loading a locally-downloaded OS image file into Raspberry Pi Imager 2.x, it correctly assumes "init_format": "none" ... create a local OS manifest using create_local_json.py', 'The latest Raspberry Pi OS Trixie images use "init_format": "cloudinit-rpi"'. doc/local_json/README.md: 'App Options > Content Repository > EDIT > Use custom file ... or launch Imager with rpi-imager --repo path/to/os_list_local.rpi-imager-manifest'. src/customization_generator.cpp: '/usr/lib/raspberrypi-sys-mods/imager_custom set_hostname', '/usr/lib/userconf-pi/userconf'. src/fastbootflashthread.cpp: writes BOOT+'meta-data'/'user-data'/'network-config', 'ds=nocloud cmdline'. https://github.com/raspberrypi/rpi-preseed README: 'Status: Prototype. Not yet production-hardened.' archive.raspberrypi.com trixie arm64 Packages lists cloud-init 25.2-1~bpo13+1+rpt20, rpi-cloud-init-mods 1:20260119, raspberrypi-sys-mods 1:20260914, and no rpi-preseed. README of rpi-image-gen: 'This image intentionally has login passwords disabled.'

claims.claim: raspi-config's Overlay File System on Trixie works the same way as on Bookworm (identical enable_overlayfs code). It installs the Debian 'overlayroot' package (cloud-initramfs-tools 0.18.debian14, an initramfs-tools script, so an initramfs is required) and prepends 'overlayroot=tmpfs ' to cmdline.txt. Boot write-protect is a sed that inserts ',ro' after 'defaults' on the /boot/firmware line of /etc/fstab, and it cannot be changed while the overlay is active. It refuses on systems with 256 MB RAM or less ('At least 512MB of RAM is recommended'). It is scriptable: 'raspi-config nonint do_overlayfs 0' enables and '... 1' disables (nonint simply runs "$@"). When the overlay is not active, the same argument is also applied to the boot-ro question, so 'nonint do_overlayfs 0' enables both the overlay and the read-only boot partition.
claims.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RPi-Distro/raspi-config/trixie/raspi-config: enable_overlayfs(): 'is_installed overlayroot || apt-get install -y overlayroot', 'sed -i $CMDLINE -e "s/^/overlayroot=tmpfs /"', '-le 262144 ... At least 512MB of RAM is recommended'. enable_bootro(): 'sed -i /etc/fstab -e "s#\(.*/boot$FIRMWARE.*\)defaults\(.*\)#\1defaults,ro\2#"'. do_overlayfs(): 'RET=$1' used for both questions; 'This cannot be changed while an overlay file system is enabled'. nonint() { "$@" }. A diff of enable_overlayfs between the bookworm and trixie branches is empty. Debian trixie Packages: 'Package: overlayroot Source: cloud-initramfs-tools Version: 0.18.debian14 Depends: cryptsetup, cryptsetup-bin, initramfs-tools'.

claims.claim: With raspi-config's default 'overlayroot=tmpfs' (recurse=1), overlayroot rewrites /etc/fstab inside the overlay. Every non-vfat, non-virtual entry, including an ext4 /data, is mounted read-only under /media/root-ro and covered by an overlay whose upper layer is on tmpfs, so writes to /data would be silently lost on reboot. vfat entries such as /boot/firmware are left as written. Two fixes work. (a) Use 'overlayroot=tmpfs:recurse=0' on the kernel command line. The command line is read last and overrides /etc/overlayroot.conf, and recurse is parsed only from the overlayroot value. raspi-config's disable regex removes only 'overlayroot=tmpfs ', so we toggle it with our own script. (b) Keep /data out of /etc/fstab and mount it with a systemd data.mount unit, since overlayroot only rewrites fstab. Using both is the most robust choice.
claims.evidence: Debian source cloud-initramfs-tools 0.18.debian14 (https://sources.debian.org/src/cloud-initramfs-tools/0.18.debian14/overlayroot/): etc/overlayroot.conf: '* recurse: default: 1 ... if set to 1, then all filesystems will be mounted read-only. if set to 0, only root will be set to read-only, and changes to other filesystems will be permenant'. scripts/init-bottom/overlayroot overlayrootify_fstab(): 'vfat|fat) use_orig="fs-unsupported"', 'if [ "$recurse" != "0" -o "$file" = "/" ]; then ... echo "$ro_line"; echo "$oline"' (overlay line with upperdir under root_rw); config files read in order 00-builtin, 10-initramfs, 20-root-config, 30-root-local-config, 90-kernel; 'recurse=${_RET_common_recurse:-1}' parsed from the overlayroot= value. Corroborated by https://github.com/raspberrypi/bookworm-feedback/issues/137 (with overlay enabled, all mounted partitions except /boot become read-only and a separate data partition is unusable).

claims.claim: Building the image with the overlay already enabled is technically possible: install overlayroot, put 'overlayroot=tmpfs:recurse=0' in cmdline.txt, 'ro' on /boot/firmware in fstab, and ship an initramfs. It is not advisable. Imager's firstrun.sh edits cmdline.txt and deletes itself from the boot partition; cloud-init keeps its instance state in /var/lib/cloud; systemd's first-boot logic and machine-id, SSH host-key regeneration, set_partuuid/resize and /data growth all write to root or boot. Under a pre-enabled overlay those writes go to RAM: they are redone on every boot, and they fail where the boot partition is read-only. Ship the overlay disabled and seal on first boot instead: a oneshot that runs after customisation has finished enables the overlay and read-only boot, then reboots.
claims.evidence: Inferred from O05 (Imager writes to the boot partition and cmdline.txt), O11 (set_partuuid remounts boot rw and edits cmdline.txt/fstab; rpi-resize.service has ConditionFirstBoot=yes) and overlayroot's tmpfs upper (O07). raspi-config get_bootro_now/enable_overlayfs show it must remount /boot/firmware rw to edit cmdline.txt. Not tested on hardware.

claims.claim: RAM use: overlayroot mounts its tmpfs with no size option, so the kernel default applies: a cap of 50% of RAM, about 450 MB on a 1 GB Pi 3. Memory is used only for data actually written to the root, so the risk is unbounded writers, not the overlay itself. Mitigations: journald Storage=volatile with RuntimeMaxUse, or a journal on /data. Podman graphroot on /data, because the overlay storage driver cannot use an overlayfs root. Podman's image_copy_tmp_dir defaults to /var/tmp, which under the overlay is RAM; set it to a /data path so image pulls do not fill memory. Run apt only in maintenance mode.
claims.evidence: overlayroot.conf: 'A tmpfs mount will be created, and usable filesystem can grow to 1/2 available memory.' scripts/init-bottom/overlayroot: 'mount -t tmpfs tmpfs-root "${root_rw}"' (no size=). https://github.com/containers/common/blob/main/docs/containers.conf.5.md: '**image_copy_tmp_dir**="/var/tmp" Default location for storing temporary container image content.' containers-storage.conf(5): graphroot default '/var/lib/containers/storage'; runroot 'should be on a tmpfs'. raspi-config: 'At least 512MB of RAM is recommended for overlay filesystem'.

claims.claim: Maintenance mode works with this sequence. (1) Remove the overlayroot= parameter from cmdline.txt; this needs a temporary 'mount -o remount,rw /boot/firmware', which raspi-config also does internally. Then reboot. (2) With root writable, remount /boot/firmware rw, because kernel, firmware and initramfs updates write there. (3) Run apt update and apt full-upgrade; overlayroot stays in the regenerated initramfs because the package remains installed. (4) Sync, put the parameter back, remount boot ro and reboot. The overlayroot package also provides 'overlayroot-chroot' for changing the lower root without a reboot, but maintainer scripts and services then run in a chroot, so the reboot path is safer. During the maintenance window root and boot are writable, so power loss is not covered there: interrupted dpkg runs need 'dpkg --configure -a', and an interrupted kernel or firmware write to FAT can stop the system booting. Document this and keep the window short.
claims.evidence: raspi-config trixie disable_overlayfs(): remounts /boot rw, 'sed -i $CMDLINE -e "s/\(.*\)overlayroot=tmpfs \(.*\)/\1\2/"', remounts ro; enable_bootro/disable_bootro refuse 'Overlay in use; cannot update fstab'. The overlayroot fstab header written by overlayrootify_fstab says: 'To permanently modify this (or any other file), you should change-root into a writable view of the underlying filesystem using: sudo overlayroot-chroot'. Power-loss statements are reasoning, not tested.

claims.claim: How Raspberry Pi OS Trixie expands on first boot. pi-gen puts 'resize' in cmdline.txt and enables rpi-resize.service. raspberrypi-sys-mods (pios/trixie, 1:20260914) ships two initramfs scripts. local-premount/resize_early: if ' resize' is in /proc/cmdline and the root partition is number 2, it runs 'parted resizepart 2 <end of disk>'. local-bottom/set_partuuid: it randomises the MBR disk ID from /dev/hwrng, rewrites PARTUUIDs in fstab and cmdline.txt, and removes ' resize' from cmdline.txt. rpi-resize.service (ConditionFirstBoot=yes) then pulls in systemd-growfs-root.service and fstrim and disables itself. To turn this off, leave 'resize' out of cmdline.txt; then neither initramfs script acts. The cost is that the disk ID is no longer randomised, which does not matter for a single device. rpi-image-gen's core layers contain no resize/growpart/growfs logic, so its images do not auto-expand; only a contrib CM5 example adds its own growpart service.
claims.evidence: https://github.com/RPi-Distro/pi-gen (master, RELEASE default 'trixie') stage1/00-boot-files/files/cmdline.txt: '... rootfstype=ext4 fsck.repair=yes rootwait resize'; stage2/01-sys-tweaks/01-run.sh: 'systemctl enable rpi-resize'. https://github.com/RPi-Distro/raspberrypi-sys-mods/tree/pios/trixie initramfs-tools/scripts/local-premount/resize_early: 'if ! grep -q \' resize\' /proc/cmdline; then exit 0', 'if [ "$ROOT_PART_NUM" -eq 2 ]; then do_resize', 'parted -m "$ROOT_DEV" u s resizepart'. local-bottom/set_partuuid: 'dd if=/dev/hwrng "of=$ROOT_DEV" bs=4 seek=110', 'sed -i \'s| resize||g\' /run/new_diskid/cmdline.txt'. debian/raspberrypi-sys-mods.rpi-resize.service: 'ConditionFirstBoot=yes', 'Wants=first-boot-complete.target systemd-growfs-root.service fstrim.service', 'ExecStartPost=/usr/bin/systemctl disable %n'. changelog 1:20250919: 'Move partition resize and trim from initramfs to systemd'. rpi-image-gen: a grep for growfs|growpart|resize2fs|expand matches only contrib/src/cm5-programming-jig.

claims.claim: Creating p3 in the image and growing it on first boot fits rpi-image-gen better than creating it on the device. Build p3 as a small ext4 partition (label DATA, for example 256 MB, optionally pre-filled from the rootfs /data subtree through genimage mountpoint), placed last. Add a first-boot oneshot ordered before data.mount that runs 'growpart /dev/mmcblk0 3' (cloud-guest-utils) or 'parted -s ... resizepart 3 100%', then grow the filesystem with resize2fs, or with the x-systemd.growfs mount option (systemd-growfs grows the filesystem only, not the partition). systemd-repart cannot be used because it supports GPT only, and Pi 3 needs MBR.
claims.evidence: genimage partitions take 'size' and 'mountpoint' (rpi-image-gen image/*/genimage.cfg.in.*). The rpi-image-gen contrib CM5 jig README (contrib/src/cm5-programming-jig/README.adoc) does the same for root: '`growpart` (from `cloud-guest-utils`) extends the root partition to the end of the disk, then `resize2fs` grows the ext4 filesystem', '(`systemd-repart` is not used: it is GPT-only ...)'. The exact unit has not been tested.

claims.claim: ext4 options for /data: keep the defaults data=ordered, commit=5 and barriers on. Add noatime, and optionally errors=remount-ro and fsck pass 2 so systemd-fsck runs on boot. Do not use data=journal: it disables delayed allocation and O_DIRECT, and the current mainline documentation marks it deprecated, with removal planned for January 2028. Power-loss safety for config and state files must come from the application: write a temp file, fsync, rename(), then fsync the directory. Optionally create the filesystem with fast_commit to make fsync cheaper.
claims.evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/Documentation/admin-guide/ext4.rst: 'data=journal ... Enabling this mode will disable delayed allocation and O_DIRECT support. This feature is deprecated and support will be removed in January 2028.'; 'commit=nrsec (*) ... The default value is 5 seconds. This means that if you lose your power, you will lose as much as the latest 5 seconds of metadata changes (your filesystem will not be damaged though, thanks to the journaling)'; 'auto_da_alloc ... broken applications don't use fsync() when replacing existing files'. Documentation/filesystems/ext4/journal.rst: fast commits in data=ordered 'needs to be enabled at mkfs time'. The deprecation note is newer than the search index, which found no second confirmation; the advice to avoid data=journal does not depend on it.

claims.claim: Mounting the FAT boot partition read-only makes it safe against power loss at runtime, because nothing writes to it. overlayroot leaves vfat fstab lines untouched, so the 'ro' flag still applies under the overlay. The remaining risk is during writes: first-boot customisation and maintenance-mode kernel or firmware updates. Do not rely on raspi-config's boot-ro sed with rpi-image-gen's fstab. That fstab has 'vfat defaults,rw,noatime,errors=remount-ro'; the sed turns it into 'defaults,ro,rw,...', and since the later 'rw' should win, raspi-config would report 'read-only' while the partition stays writable. Write 'ro' explicitly in our own setup.sh fstab.
claims.evidence: overlayroot overlayrootify_fstab(): 'vfat|fat) use_orig="fs-unsupported"' then 'echo "$line # $MYTAG:$use_orig"' (original line kept). rpi-image-gen image/mbr/simple_dual/setup.sh: '$BOOTDEV  /boot/firmware  vfat defaults,rw,noatime,errors=remount-ro 0 2'. raspi-config enable_bootro sed inserts 'defaults,ro'; get_bootro_conf greps 'defaults.*,ro[ ,]'. That the later 'rw' wins is based on mount(8) option processing and was not tested.

claims.claim: A/B for later. The official documentation says 'All Raspberry Pi models support tryboot'. The autoboot.txt page names no model restriction, but its A/B example uses six partitions (bootfs, boot A/B, root A/B, data), which is more than MBR's four primary partitions, and Pi 3 has no GPT boot support in rpi-image-gen. rpi-image-gen's ready-made A/B layout (image-rota, GPT) is limited to cm4|pi4|cm5|pi5. A/B on Pi 3 would need extended/logical MBR partitions and is unverified. In practice, A/B is supported on Pi 4/5.
claims.evidence: https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html (Fail-safe OS updates (tryboot)): 'All Raspberry Pi models support tryboot' (only caveat: Pi 4B rev 1.0/1.1 EEPROM must not be write protected). https://github.com/raspberrypi/documentation/blob/master/documentation/asciidoc/computers/config_txt/autoboot.adoc: example layout 'Partition 1 (FAT) ... Partition 6: An optional persistent data partition'. rpi-image-gen image/gpt/ab_userdata/image.yaml: 'X-Env-VarRequires-Valid: string,regex:^(cm4|pi4|cm5|pi5)$'.

claims.claim: pi-gen as an alternative: it builds the official Raspberry Pi OS images (default RELEASE trixie; master branch ARCH=armhf, a separate arm64 branch), so 32-bit armhf is first-class and the result is exactly Raspberry Pi OS, including the cloud-init stage with rpi-cloud-init-mods and rpi-resize. Its export-image step hard-codes two MBR partitions with parted, so p3 needs a patched export stage. It covers the 32-bit Pi 3 case but is less modular than rpi-image-gen.
claims.evidence: https://github.com/RPi-Distro/pi-gen master build.sh: 'export RELEASE=${RELEASE:-trixie}', 'export ARCH=armhf'; branches include 'arm64'. export-image/prerun.sh: 'parted --script "${IMG_FILE}" mklabel msdos', 'mkpart primary fat32 ...', 'mkpart primary ext4 ...'. stage2/04-cloud-init/00-packages: 'cloud-init', 'rpi-cloud-init-mods'. rpi-image-gen README: 'For the tool used to create the Raspberry Pi OS distribution, please go to https://github.com/RPi-Distro/pi-gen'.

recommendation: Build: rpi-image-gen in GitHub Actions on runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm, the same as upstream CI, with './rpi-image-gen build -S brewberry-os/ -c brewberry-os/config/<board>.yaml'. Build arm64 only and drop the 32-bit goal. Pi 3 and Pi 4 share the rpi-generic64 device family; Pi 5 needs rpi5/2712, so either build two images (pi3+pi4, pi5) or write one custom device layer that installs both kernels, as Raspberry Pi OS does. Base it on trixie-minbase plus layers for network-manager, openssh-server and podman (our own layer installing podman, crun, netavark and aardvark-dns), overlayroot, initramfs-tools, cloud-guest-utils, cloud-init + rpi-cloud-init-mods (for Imager init_format 'cloudinit-rpi'; alternatively raspberrypi-sys-mods + userconf-pi for 'systemd'). Publish a .rpi-imager-manifest / os_list JSON with init_format next to each release so Imager offers customisation. Layout: a custom image layer copied from image/mbr/simple_dual with MBR p1 vfat /boot/firmware about 512 MB, p2 ext4 / fixed at about 3-4 GB, and p3 ext4 label DATA starting small (about 256 MB), mounted at /data. setup.sh writes fstab: '/boot/firmware vfat ro,noatime,errors=remount-ro 0 2' and '/ ext4 ro,...'. /data is NOT in fstab; it is mounted by data.mount (Options=noatime,errors=remount-ro, plus x-systemd.growfs, or resize2fs from the grow unit). cmdline.txt has NO 'resize' token and no overlayroot at build time. First boot: (1) Imager/cloud-init customisation applies normally (root and boot are writable). (2) brewberry-growdata.service (Before=data.mount, stamp-guarded) runs 'growpart /dev/mmcblk0 3' and resize2fs. (3) A /data layout service creates /data/containers/storage (storage.conf graphroot), /data/tmp (containers.conf image_copy_tmp_dir), /data/config and /data/update. (4) brewberry-firstload loads the preloaded OCI archive shipped in /usr/share/brewberrypi into Podman. (5) brewberry-seal.service runs after cloud-final/first-boot-complete.target: it prepends 'overlayroot=tmpfs:recurse=0' to cmdline.txt and reboots. From then on root is overlay-on-tmpfs, boot is ro, and /data is rw ext4 (data=ordered, commit=5, noatime); journald is volatile with RuntimeMaxUse capped, or persisted to /data/log. The application writes config atomically (tmp + fsync + rename + dir fsync). Maintenance mode (our own script 'brewberry-maint on|off', not raspi-config): 'on' remounts boot rw, removes the overlayroot param and reboots. Then apt update && apt full-upgrade with /boot/firmware remounted rw. 'off' re-adds the param, remounts boot ro and reboots. Power safety does not hold during the maintenance window; document that. Verify on hardware: initramfs present and overlayroot active (findmnt /, /media/root-rw); /data mounted rw from the real device; pulling the plug in each state.
open_questions: Can one arm64 image boot Pi 3, Pi 4 and Pi 5 (both kernel8.img and kernel_2712.img plus all DTBs in one boot partition), or do we publish two images (pi3/pi4 and pi5)? rpi-image-gen's pi5 device layer uses rpi-linux-2712 while pi3/pi4 use rpi-generic64.
Is dropping 32-bit acceptable? rpi-image-gen has only armhf building blocks, no device layer. A 32-bit Pi 3 image would mean pi-gen (master = armhf) or a hand-made device layer.

Which Imager init_format should we use: cloudinit-rpi (matches current Raspberry Pi OS Trixie; cloud-init adds RAM and boot time on a Pi 3) or systemd/firstrun.sh (lighter; needs raspberrypi-sys-mods + userconf-pi)? Needs a test flash to confirm Imager 2.x behaviour with a manifest pointing at our release URL.

Does rpi-image-gen's image-rpios layout with the rpi-generic64 kernel actually produce and boot an initramfs (config.txt template has auto_initramfs=1; kernel layer env INITRD: "No")? overlayroot needs an initramfs. Check on the first CI build.
Do ubuntu-24.04-arm hosted runners cost money or have limits for a private repository? Free availability was confirmed only for upstream's public repository workflow.

Is the deprecation note for ext4 data=journal (removal January 2028) in mainline docs already in the Raspberry Pi 6.12/6.x kernel docs? Not decision-relevant, because data=journal is not recommended anyway.

Is power loss during first boot (growpart/resize2fs, cloud-init, seal reboot) and during maintenance mode acceptable, or do we need a recovery path (for example, the seal service retries until it succeeds, and maintenance runs only on explicit user action)?
Does autoboot.txt partition-level A/B work on Pi 3 with MBR logical partitions? Unverified. Upstream tooling targets only Pi 4/5.
